subtopic: NATO-POSSIBLE REASSESSMENT OF CANADA'S MILITARY ROLE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Prime Minister a question regarding the NATO council conference which will be taking place in a few days. I ask whether the Canadian government is proposing to reassess Canada's military role in NATO. If so, does Canada intend to suggest the phasing out of the CF-104 squadrons; does it propose any replacement of these by another type of aircraft; and finally, does Canada intend to suggest the transfer of the infantry brigade or any part of it to a reserve position?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: NATO-POSSIBLE REASSESSMENT OF CANADA'S MILITARY ROLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at each annual meeting of the NATO council it is customary to review not only the force plans of the member governments but the policies of NATO countries themselves and the direction in which the alliance should be moving.
That will happen in Brussels next week. I believe there will be a report before the counail, called the Harmel report after the foreign minister of Belgium who has been working on it with others, on the goals of the alliance. That will be considered as well as the force plans of member governments. So far as I know there is no proposal before the council which will change radically the force goals or the objectives of NATO. I do not think there is any reason to expect radical changes in Canada's contribution to NATO at this time.

speechtext:
My question is for the Minister of Finance. Is it the intention of the government to extend beyond the present effective expiry date of January 1, 1968 the income tax regulation permitting industry an accelerated depreciation rate on equipment installed to prevent, reduce or eliminate water pollution? If so,

will the government consider similar encouragement to industry to take action regarding air and soil pollution?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: TAX INCENTIVES TO PLANTS INSTALLING CORRECTIVE DEVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this question has been asked previously by the hon. member for Essex South and by other hon. members, I believe. The government is giving consideration to the extension of the regulations affecting water pollution after January 1, 1968. I hope I will be able to make a definite announcement before the consideration of the budget is concluded.
With regard to the second part of the question, I have received many representations with regard to similar treatment in connection with air and soil pollution. The matter is under consideration, but I should say that it is of a different character. The regulations permitting an accelerated depreciation on water pollution devices and systems are in the law now and we have to make a decision about their extension. With regard to expenditures on air and soil pollution control, this is a new matter which requires very careful consideration before new action is taken.

subtopic: TAX INCENTIVES TO PLANTS INSTALLING CORRECTIVE DEVICES
speechtext: I have a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. subtopic: TAX INCENTIVES TO PLANTS INSTALLING CORRECTIVE DEVICES
speechtext: One of the reasons I hesitate to make more than just an announcement is that the point raised by the hon. member is being given consideration. I will make a definite announcement on it before the budget debate is over. The purpose of putting in a date was to induce industry to take action as quickly as possible. If you make this a permanent feature it changes the nature of the incentive. Therefore I agree with the hon. member that we have to decide one way or the other, whether it is for an interim period or indefinitely.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Finance. I wonder whether the minister could now answer the question I asked first on November 10 and which he said he would answer in his budget speech, and which when that was not done I repeated last Friday, in connection with how successful the

December 7, 19G7
Inquiries of the Ministry Canadian savings bond campaign had been in comparison with former years, and particularly how much new money the minister estimated would come in from this source.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO RESULTS OF RECENT BOND ISSUE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have had this reply on my desk for two or three days, and I was hoping the hon. member would ask his question again. In my budget speech last Thursday I mentioned that the Canada savings bond campaign had succeeded in raising a substantial amount of new cash during November despite the very adverse circumstances under which it had to be carried on. In general the sale of Canada savings bonds lived up to our sober expectations. We could not, under the circumstances that prevail, have expected that this would be a resounding success; in fact it has been a comparative success.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker,-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order. Maybe there could be a little less conversation in the house so we can hear the remarks of the hon. member for York South.

subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have only a few minutes left. I argued yesterday that the budget before the house was inequitable in the taxes which it imposed as well as in the taxes which it failed to impose if the minister was convinced that he required added revenue at this time and that he could not wait until the regular budget next spring. Second, Mr. Speaker, I argued that the budget will not accomplish even the purposes which the minister said he wanted to accomplish. Third, and I suggested that this was the most iniquitous part of the budget, I argued that it is likely to slow down the economy and to create additional unemployment. Indeed, I suggested that this was one of the explicit and implicit objectives of the budget.
Today, Mr. Speaker, I want to suggest that another significant key to the thinking of the government is the cavalier way in which the Carter recommendations have been thrown into the ash can. The Carter report, I remind you, sir, makes a ringing indictment of our present tax system. To use its own words, it finds that system "inequitable in many important respects." It goes on to say that the combined effect of the various taxes, and again I use its words, is "such that low income individuals and families pay higher

December 7, 1967
The Budget-Mr. Lewis taxes than is equitable when compared to middle and upper income individuals and families." Members of our party have been saying this for many years, and now it has been confirmed by an unassailable authority.
The point I want to make is that the government has before it a report made after years of study and analysis of many aspects of our economic life. Its conclusion is that our present tax system is unjust and inequitable. It makes very specific proposals for new fields of taxations and for the shifting of the burden from the low income to the higher income groups in the community. The Carter commission, in our view, is right when it said that the objective of equity in taxation should have a higher priority than most or all other objectives.
I think that the chairman of that commission and his colleagues must be admired and congratulated for making an equitable tax system their major consideration and guide. I appreciate that the recommendations of the report are radical and that some of them are complex, but I say that when we have a system which men of intelligence and integrity have found to be unjust and inequitable then it is surely time to change the system instead of trying to patch it up here and there.
I saw Mr. Carter on television on budget night. I was impressed by his thoughtful manner. If I remember correctly, in very measured tones he bluntly accused the government of having yielded to the lobbies and pressures of the special interests, and he named them:	oil, mining, insurance, and
similar interests.
So far as I have knowledge of the matter, and of course I do not have all knowledge, it is significant that the organizations representing the ordinary people of Canada, such as labour unions and the like, have all supported the basic philosophy of the Carter report, even though they may have expressed reservations on one or two details. They asked the government to implement the report but apparently their voice was not heard. The voice of the powerful prevailed, as usual, with this government. This, I suggest, is a great pity and a great injustice.
I want to conclude by making one final point as forcefully as I can. During the current year we have had a resurgence of pride in our country, justifiable pride. Unfortunately we have also had disturbing signs of continuing division. All of us in Canada, of all political parties and faiths, are determined to

make every effort to overcome divisive influences in our country and to strengthen the unity and the purposefulness of our nation and our people in every part and in every province.
I venture to warn the government that economic policies such as are represented in this budget may do harm not only to the economy but to the great effort toward national unity and understanding, for I suggest it is clear that any reduction in economic activity, any increase in unemployment, any curtailment of government economic participation will have a larger and deeper adverse effect in those parts of the country which are already at a disadvantage compared with other parts. Such policies, in my submission, cannot but aggravate the regional inequalities in economic and social opportunities. This can do more to harm progress toward an integrated and meaningful Canadian unity than most other factors. It is for all these reasons that I moved the amendment which is in your hands, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is without taking into account the municipal taxes.

subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, yes. We are talking about federal taxes right now; municipal, provincial and school taxes have to be added.
I will give you an example, based on my personal experience. I have a house in Hull, financed by the Mutual Life Company of Canada, and at the end of the year, I was given a balance sheet or statement of account, indicating I had remitted $1,536. Out of this amount, over $800 went for interests, and over $600 for taxes, so that, at the end of the year, I had repaid only $206, I think, of the capital on my house.

subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why did you not buy it cash?

subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Champlain is asking me why I did not buy it cash? For the same reason as all other Canadians, because cash purchase of a house is beyond our means. That is why we take financing plans, why all Canadians are more or less in the same boat.
December 7, 1967

The Budget-Mr. Caouette
Mr. Speaker, I said a while ago that the government was bringing in some projects designed to impoverish Canadians rather than help them. One of the highlights of the mini-budget, according to the press release of the Department of Finance, is the following and I quote:
Anti-inflationary measures will be taken under the form of a drastic reduction of expenses and an increase of tax revenues, in order to make up almost entirely any budget deficit in 1968-69.
The minister states that they are anti-inflationary measures. In my opinion, a reduction of expenses and an increase of tax revenues can only mean a tax increase.
Now, when Canadians are deprived of their purchasing power and prices remain unchanged or tend to go up, are we fighting against inflation, or are we not rather promoting inflation? In the same press release, we also read:
The government will reduce expenses concerning many items of the budget and it will reduce its loans within the program aimed at controlling inflation, lessening pressures on the capital market and minimizing tax increases.
Mr. Speaker, while it is stated that tax increases will be minimized, for the second consecutive time, a tax increase has been announced. And does the government believe that by doing so it is fighting inflation? If the works in progress are stopped, if projects are left in abeyance, it is obvious that the number of unemployed will increase in Canada. If the number of unemployed increases, those people will be unable to pay taxes as they are doing at the present time.
The tax system will have to be adjusted once again by increasing taxes for those who are still earning something. This means that we are living under an absurd system that does not take realities into consideration.
The Minister of Finance knows-as we have been saying time and again in the house-that instead of adjusting the monetary system to the physical potential of Canada, an attempt is being made to adjust the economic system to the financial possibilities, that is, the opposite of common sense. In private industry, in trade, in business, it is normal to adjust one's budget to one's financial resources. But, for a sovereign

government, responsible for the monetary policy of a country like ours, to bow to the demand of such a system is a paradox, and quite inconceivable.
The minister is willing to reduce all sorts of things to fight inflation, but does he reduce the interest we are paying this year on the national debt, namely $1,300 million? He does not say anything about the interest we pay financiers, not one word. But the little man pays a surtax of 5 per cent on his income tax, and that is logical. Increasing federal tax on alchohol and tobacco again is normal. Reducing or slowing down the public works of the federal government is also logical, but we still continue to pay our tribute to the financial system.
According to the news release, the minister also said:
A special surtax is proposed: 5 per cent on the basic income tax as from January 1, 1968; this will not apply to the low income taxpayer, because an exemption is provided for on the first $100 of basic income tax.
The average Canadian must pay about $300 or $350 in income tax a year, which means that there will be an increase of about $20 a year. Some might say that it is not so much, but $20 for someone who already does not have enough, who actually is short, it is already a lot, and the minister does not take that into consideration.
Federal taxes on spirits and tobacco are raised by 10 per cent. In this case, we get this answer: Well, those who do not want to pay such a tax simply do not have to buy liquor and they can stop smoking. It is an answer as good as any, but personally it is not a tax which worries me a lot.
Now, when the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) said that it was again an attack against the small wage-earner, I feel that it is not so much the little man as the companies which will be the most affected, because they are the ones which make a lot of money and which, as a rule, buy most often from the liquor boards of the various provinces of Canada. They will help pay a share of that tax.
But I think that the tax restraints which are apparently essential to avoid a possibly
December 7, 19S7

serious recession represent the main point in the budget. However, when the minister said:
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
After parliament has taken the necessary fiscal measures, the government intends to implement a program aimed at mobilizing public opinion-
It is to be expected that thousands of dollars will be spent on radio, television and newspaper advertising.
-in favour of voluntary, concerted restraints in respect to prices, costs and wage increases.
All Canadians will be invited to limit their activities, not to build right away; instead of "Do it now", it will be: "Do it later", wait till our financial situation is stabilized, wait till people slow down their way of life, then, we will be able to launch again the feverish rush of prices toward wages, of wages toward prices, as is the case since this government has been in power and, furthermore, as it was under the previous administration.
Another point is that fiscal reform will consist mostly in altering the present system instead of adopting completely different methods. What does this mean?
Instead of taxing on the one hand, they will be taxing on the other. But what about compression, restriction in the area of government expenses? The expenditures of the Department of National Defence may possibly be restrained to transfer or lend the amount saved to another department, but another department is asked to reduce its expenditures to the utmost in order to help another department or ministry. These are alterations and not new methods. One point remains nevertheless: we are still fooling around with a vitiated and vicious system and the Minister of Finance will not take a single step to get us out of such a system. Efforts are still being made to adjust the economic potential to the financial assets instead of adjusting the finances to the economic needs of the people, and that is where the fault lies in the whole system.
A former president of the United States used to say and I quote:
If the American people ever allow the private banks to control the issue of money, first through inflation then through deflation, the banks and the companies growing around them will despoil the citizens of their properties until their children wake up without a home on the continent their forefathers conquered.
The Budget-Mr. Caouette
Mr. Speaker, what Thomas Jefferson said in the United States 160 years ago we can repeat today in Canada, because we are truly being completely robbed of what our Canadian ancestors have helped to build and have left us as a common heritage, as a cultural heritage, as a material heritage, in short as a heritage from all points of view.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance mentioned three urgent and closely related objectives:	first, to restrain the inflationary
increases in prices, costs and cost of living that are undermining our prosperity; to ease the disturbing strains in the capital market that threaten our continued economic growth; and to meet in a non-inflationary way the costs of continuing public programs essential to social security and long-run national development.
The first objective suggests restraining the inflationary increases that are undermining our prosperity. At this point, we must pay the piper, a situation the minister himself had foreseen in his June 1967 budget. But the measures he proposed then have proved to be most inadequate.
The second objective is aimed at easing the disturbing strains in the capital market that threaten our continued economic growth. Here again, the same problem as in June 1967 is being faced. The solutions then applied by the minister have proved ineffective and ill-advised.
The third objective asks us to meet the costs of social security measures. But, in his present budget, the minister tells us that the implementation of medicare will require further tax increases or the imposition of a new tax to enable the Canadian people to afford medicare, and it is on that point that I found the speech made yesterday by the hon. member for York South completely inconsistent. He blamed the government for imposing taxes, but he felt it should change its fiscal methods, while retaining the present financial system.
He added that we needed a medicare system, better pensions for veterans, eflftcient economic planning and a system of priorities, all that thanks to increased taxes. But the hon. member for York South did not say who or where to tax, except, of course, large companies which, in turn, would increase
December 7, 1967

The Budget-Mr. Caouette prices and, finally, the taxes would again be paid by the Canadian people, the Canadian worker.
The third objective is to foot the bill for welfare measures, like the Canada Pension Plan, but through non-inflationary measures. That is unacceptable, in my opinion.
First, Canada's economic situation does not allow us, as legislators, to promote a full and adequate program of social security. It allows us only to give with one hand and take back with the other, and in the end, that is taxation. According to the Minister of Finance, taxation is one thing only: the right to levy taxes, to empty the pockets of the Canadian taxpayers. That is taxation.
And when the provincial premiers meet in Toronto or Ottawa, as they did in Toronto recently, the first question that arises is that of taxation. As far as a new Canadian constitution is concerned, it is not so much a matter of deciding if French or English is to be spoken, but rather of deciding if the provincial governments or the federal government will continue to dig deeper in the pockets of the Canadian citizens. Here is what the new confederation, the new constitution is all about: taxation.
In fact, as soon as the representatives of the provinces parted in Toronto, the Minister of Finance introduced his budget in which he told us that he needed more money and that he was going to take it out of the pockets of the Canadian taxpayers.
The day before yesterday, the Quebec premier stated about the same thing. Word for word he said that we could not spend any more and that the people of Quebec must be resigned to accept tax increases soon.
The municipalities and school boards are in the same situation. Instead of going to the monetary source, where money is made, the minister goes where there is none and he says: everyone must reduce his expenses. In fact, he tells the school boards: stop building schools; to the municipalities: stop expanding; to the provinces: try to cut down your expenses to the strict minimum, and to us in Ottawa, we shall do the same thing.
But, when everyone is tightening his belt, the financial system continues to rob everyone, as it has done since confederation. That is the ailment of this confederation.

What will they do with the unemployed? They do not know. There is not a single program put forward by this government to take care of those who, this winter, will become unemployed as a direct result of the budget. The unemployed will simply have time to make more unemployed.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, we all remember, besides, December 16, 1966-almost a year ago- when the Minister of Finance said he had a wonderful Christmas present for the elderly of Canada. He forgot to add, however, that all Canadians would have to contribute to that gift. As a matter of fact, the increase in the old age pension was adopted and implemented, but it is not the government that paid for it; the Canadian taxpayers did, and the Bank of Canada did not intervene at all.
Let us briefly examine the situation prevailing at present for a Canadian taxpayer. He is faced with increased prices in every field: clothing, food, transportation, automobile, maintenance costs, insurance, municipal taxes, school taxes, provincial taxes and levies, and to top it all, a 10 per cent federal tax on tobacco and spirits, as well as a 5 per cent increase in the basic personal income tax.
Each one of those increases leads to a decrease in the purchasing power of the small wage-earner. Everyone must admit it, because that is due to the system. And so, the higher the cost of living, the lower the purchasing power of the individual, and while the Minister of Finance does his best to reduce the purchasing power, the more stocks accumulate in Canada. Industries, stores, warehouses are brimming over with goods. One needs only go down Rideau Street in Ottawa, for instance, or down Bank Street, or in any city in Canada, Montreal, Sherbrooke, Lac Megantic, Rouyn-Noranda, to see how stores are splitting at the seams with goods. Special Christmas sales are being advertised even before Christmas. They no longer wait till after New Year's day. Before Christmas? Why? Because they have astounding quantities of goods. And, in the face of this production, this real state of affairs, the Minister of Finance does his utmost to reduce the purchasing power of Canadian citizens.
December 7, 1967

What logic, from the economic viewpoint. To reduce purchasing power, when the production is there, unsold, before the eyes of people who need it. Each increase brings a reduction of purchasing power. So, the more the cost of living increases, the less a person can buy.
Let us never forget that what counts is not what the taxpayer earns, but what he can buy. That is what gives the dollar, the monetary unit of a country, its value. I should think that the Minister of Finance is smart enough to understand that the buyer, if his dollar is taken away from him, can no longer buy.
Today, with all that organization, all this tax system, with federal, provincial, municipal and school taxes, what about the Canadian worker, the Canadian farmer, the white collar worker, the professional, the businessman. The businessman now has to contend with the system, and the government gives the example.
The Economic Council of Canada, in its latest annual report, anticipates a rise of 7 per cent in unemployment this winter. In the face of these facts, which nobody in this house can deny, let us put the following question to ourselves: Do we seriously think that the Canadian taxpayer is now in a position to face such measures?
Anyhow, the ostensible purpose of those measures is to take the purchasing power out of the Canadian taxpayers' pockets, in order to meet the excessive government expenditures. Such is the result of election promises; the people, the humble folk always end up by footing the bill. It is easy to make promises to the people; the difficulty is to administer according to their expectations and aspirations.
The present economic system does not reach its objective because it allows this criminal anomaly: misery in the midst of affluence. As I said earlier, instead of waging war on poverty, budgets which will increase even more the number of poor people in Canada are brought down.
Our financial system, one of the tools available to distribute our products and services, is based on a false theory. That system is responsible for the economic crises which regularly and periodically shake the Canadian people.
Social Credit, under its three basic proposals, wants first of all a national currency and not a currency borrowed in the United States which forces us to beg for permission in New
The Budget-Mr. Caouette York to develop our country, Canada. In my opinion, a national currency is a currency suited to our economic needs and our physical possibilities to ensure the development of our country.
In the second place, Social Credit asks for a two-price policy instead of a tax so to facilitate the normal marketing of production for Canadians who need that production.
In the third place, the Creditistes advocate the payment of a national dividend. This makes a lot of people laugh, because it is so much the opposite to taxes.

subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleagues for having given me the opportunity to continue, during two or three minutes, so that I may state my feelings about the budget of the Minister of Finance.
I was talking about the national dividend, that is just the opposite of taxes and the taxation system. Some argue that the national dividend would promote inflation, but we maintain that it is the opposite, the antithesis of inflation and deflation, as it is the only means of maintaining a perpetual balance between purchasing power and national production, between production and services provided to the Canadian people. Taxes are the opposite of good judgment, when the dividend, which would not come from anybody's pocket, which would not increase prices and which would be paid directly by the Bank of Canada, according to Canada's economic status and the Canadian economic situation, would restore economic order, while we are now living in economic chaos.
We are going now through a period of inflation. However, we do not accept a national dividend and even less Social Credit. But we sure have inflation. Why? Because inflation results precisely from taxes and from the debt-money with which the government is administering Canada, somewhat like the example I gave a moment ago of the construction of a small $15,000 house which will cost $46,000 after 35 years. In fact, the government is at that point or, rather,
5152	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Caouette beyond that point since we will be paying this $1,300 million in interest only on the national debt or the same as the national defence budget. However, such a national debt or the interest we pay on it cannot put bread on the tables of the Canadian people.
Social Credit favours a dividend which would not be included in the prices and which would be paid directly by the Bank of Canada, according to the economic data on Canada. This dividend would restore economic order and increase the purchasing power without increasing the prices. Instead of hitting everybody with taxes while everybody has to live on credit today, the dividend would restore order, not overnight but gradually, until people would have the money required to buy the things they need.
This is, I think, the logic of an economic system which would guarantee the security and freedom of every citizen. It is for this security and freedom that the Creditistes offer their solution.
I know that some economists do not accept these solutions; they do not accept the dividend. In fact, some of them suggest that economic planning would solve the problem, where others advocate socialism as a panacea for all the economic problems of Canada.
Just yesterday, I heard the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) say: If the government would nationalize the industries, it would solve the problem. In my opinion, this would not solve anything.
Before concluding my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I should like to read the statement made by an economist from Czechoslovakia, a socialist country, as you know. I quote:
On June 7 last, during a conference delivered in Montreal, the most prominent economist of Czechoslovakia stated that, from now on, the public enterprises of his country should be economical or close their doors. Dr. Vladimir Kadlec, dean of the economics faculty at the University of Prague, added that his country was forced to introduce capitalist incentives to increase national productivity. Like Russia, Yugoslavia and other Communist countries, Czechoslovakia now recognizes that publicity, competition, personal initiative, individual ambition are tokens of prosperity. In the last five years, the national revenue has not increased a fraction of a point in Czechoslovakia and productivity has declined constantly. Moreover, the standard of living has never been so low and the cost of living so high.
Moreover, fed up with a harassing bureaucracy, disappointed by an illusory social and economic planning, the Czech workers have lost the desire to work. Those are the reasons which drove the Communist government of Czechoslovakia to borrow certain methods and economic principles from

DEBATES	December 7, 1967
the capitalist system. In spite of repeated and disastrous failures in the Communist countries, we find in our federal and provincial governments politicians who persist in leading our economy toward socialism. Under the guise of social progress, they never tire of putting to us the socialist alternative.
Mr. Speaker, we believe that private enterprise is the system which gives the best results in planning a nation's economy, because is there another one which can produce more and give a better output at the production level? So, it is up to a responsible Minister of Finance and government to organize a distribution system through a healthy Canadian money, so that all Canadian citizens will have their share of the national production, of the wealth of our country, Canada.

subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege to take part in this budget debate. It has been called a mini budget, though I believe the Canadian people understand better than at any time in recent years that mini-budget though it may be, it affects not only them personally but the whole of the Canadian economy.
I do not want to add to the statements which have already been made in one form or another about the seriousness of the situation in which we find ourselves at the present time, but I think it is imperative that it be emphasized to the government, to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) and, yes, to the Canadian people as well who may have some questions to ask concerning the financial situation at the present time, that we do in fact face very serious economic trouble. As I see the handwriting on the wall and listen to the remarks of the Minister of Finance as he rationalizes the situation in which we find ourselves and at the same time attempts to suggest the reason things are what they are and how they may be corrected. I find a great deal of similarity between the situation today toward the end of 1967 and that which existed in the closing days of 1962. The situation that developed in the early weeks of 1963 could well be a forerunner of what is going to happen in the early weeks of 1968. Certainly we do have reason for concern.
I share the concern expressed by the Minister of Finance, even though we cannot agree with the policies he is adopting or the justification for the tax increases that he has brought in. It was only last fall, if I recall correctly during the early days of September, that the economic council spoke very firmly in no uncertain terms about what it regarded
December 7, 1967

as the developing crisis. The bombshell report issued by the Economic Council stated very clearly that there was growing fear, which every day was becoming more noticeable, about what is happening in the Canadian economy. I am sure the government was not pleased at the time with what the Economic Council said, but what they said has come true and is becoming more evident day by day. Therefore the debate on this mini budget involving these tax increases and government policy, and also the statement that we expect to hear the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Benson) make tonight, are very important and are tragic evidence that all is not well.
I was interested to see a couple of articles in the London Free Press on December 2 which evidently are what we can expect when the screws are tightened as they are being tightened now. For example, one company in the London area has closed down its production of heavy road equipment in Canada altogether. The company is a subsidiary of a United States company and all production has been shifted to the parent factory in that country. Another major company in the London area hints that there will be a shutdown at some future date. Some 68 persons have been idled by cut-backs as of December 2 and perhaps more people will be laid off in a few days at a second company. This too is evidence that all is not well.
Let me bring again to the attention of the house, Mr. Speaker, those things about which I believe Canadians are most concerned. First of all, interest rates have never been so high. Just today I received a letter from my own banker indicating that interest rates have been raised on ordinary bank loans by half of 1 per cent. Only a few weeks ago we were told that the interest rate on national housing loans had reached an all-time high level of 8i per cent. The cost of money for the normal carrying on of industry and commerce and for vital and necessary construction, such as home construction, is such that it has placed an additional, very severe burden on Canadians who are facing a cost of living that is spiralling upward as never before.
Second, Mr. Speaker, this year's budgetary deficit will be the biggest in the nation's history. The Minister of Finance has talked about the increase in government income as a result of the increase in taxes, but the amount the minister can expect to gain from these taxes between now and the end of the fiscal year will not have very much effect in reducing the over-all amount of the deficit which in a year of prosperity, as our centen-
The Budget-Mr. Thompson nial year has been, is higher than at any other time in the nation's history, either in war or in peace.
This situation, Mr. Speaker, just cannot continue, and obviously something is radically wrong with our approach to the financial problems facing the country. For example, look at the housing crisis. Housing starts this year so far as unit construction is concerned are far behind. There is no hope of catching up on the lag last year. As already mentioned in this debate, the cost of housing for the people who need housing and want to own a house has increased many times as a result of the increased cost of interest. How long can we continue in this way, Mr. Speaker? We all know very well that housing is important to the well-being of our nation, not only just to the economy but to many other aspects.
I am particularly concerned about the increasing prices facing our farmers. This is creating an extremely difficult situation. Prices for farm products are not even holding their own but are tending to go down. Yet the cost of production goes up. In western Canada in particular there is a crisis because the cash crop, which the farmers normally expect to dispose of in the early months following the harvest, has no market this year. The wheat quotas are just not there. Moreover, the price of wheat has gone down and the prices for hogs and cattle are hardly holding their own. As I say, the farmers are not able to sell their cash crop to pay for their harvesting operations or even their seeding last spring. This affects the entire economy, but the western agricultural economy perhaps more than the eastern economy is finding itself in extreme difficulty.
What is the prospect, Mr. Speaker, of even maintaining our grain exports? The devaluation of the British pound has certainly cast a shadow across the prospect of maintaining wheat prices at an economic level. The devaluation of the pound will not only affect Britain and the other countries which likewise devalued because they found themselves in difficult economic circumstances but will cause these countries to lower their demand for Canadian wheat. As a result of the devaluation of the British pound Japan is finding herself facing a very critical situation, though as yet she has not devalued her own currency.

speechtext:
Before darkness descended on the house I was saying something about the difficulty that western agriculture finds itself in. Not only do we face the prospect that lower prices will be obtained for the products of western farms, and I am referring particularly to lower wheat prices, but since western grain is most important to the Canadian economy and since our western farmers face the prospect of losing markets, the entire country will suffer. Also, what is happening in China does not lead us to hope that we shall be able to continue to enjoy our grain markets in that country.
Another area which is of great concern to the economy of this country is that area of activity which relates to wages. Certain of our workers have demanded wage parity with workers in the United States. I am sure that no one in the house will begrudge any of our workers a living wage, especially in these times of rising prices. But it must be remembered that the Canadian worker is competing, so far as productivity is concerned, with the worker who lives in a nation that is more than ten times economically greater than our nation. This demand for parity will drive our cost of living ever higher and will increase the upward momentum of the inflationary spiral.
One of the greatest causes for this so-called inflation has been the unprecedented amount of government spending during recent years. The greatest factor in the inflationary problem is one which the Minister of Finance himself is responsible for creating. That factor is the enormous increase in government spending that we have witnessed during the last several years. Whether the Minister of Finance accepts the blame or not, statistics reveal that the rate of government spending at the federal level exceeds by far the rate of economic growth as well as the rate of increase in wages and the rate at which living costs are rising.
Some interesting statistics were released last week by the Canadian Economic Foun-

DEBATES	December 7, 1967
dation. They show that the 3.5 million taxpayers who earn less than $5,000 per year pay nearly 50 per cent of their income in aggregate taxes yearly to governments at one level or another.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question? Is he directing his criticisms also at provincial and municipal governments?

subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, I am, but now I am
specifically directing it to the Minister of Finance. My criticism applies to governments at all levels. In his last two budget speeches at least the Minister of Finance has asked governments at provincial and municipal levels to exercise restraint. Yet he has permitted federal spending to run wild. The rate of increase in costs of government at all levels has been greater than the rate of productivity increase in this country. I venture to say that federal spending has grown at a greater rate than provincial and municipal spending.
The statistic released by the Canadian Economic Foundation reveal that the 1.6 million taxpayers who earn between $5,000 and $10,000 a year pay more than 50 per cent of their income in taxes. The average tax payment for that group amounts to $5,300. That amount is paid in aggregate taxes to governments at all levels.
The taxpayers' union reports that today the average taxpayer pays about half his income in taxes which include personal income tax, sales tax, property tax, automobile licences and all forms of hidden tax which pay for the cost of government. I have some statistics for 1965 which support the contentions of the Canadian Economic Foundation and the taxpayers' union. I could not get detailed statistics for 1966 but unfortunately government spending for that year reached an even higher level than in previous years. The figures for 1965 relate to net national income.
As at December 31, 1965, the gross national product of Canada was $52,056 million. As at December 31, 1965, our net national income was $38,940 million. This figure includes wages, salaries, commissions, income from the sale of products and from all other sources. In the fiscal year ended March 31, 1966, the interest that we paid on our debt amounted to $1,051.3 million. Also, in the fiscal year ended March 31, 1966, our direct national debt was $27,617 million, an increase over 1964-65 of $1,044 million. Bringing these figures down to a daily basis, I point out that the daily interest cost of our national debt
December 7, 1967

amounted to $2,881,121.30. The hourly cost was more than $120,000, and the cost per minute was approximately $2,000.
The truly alarming statistic is that which shows that federal, provincial and municipal expenditures in 1965 reached the astronomical total of $22,500 million. Of this amount the federal government spent $7,633 million or 34 per cent, the provincial governments spent $5,220 million or 23.3 per cent, and the municipal governments spent $9,596 million or 42.7 per cent.
Taking these costs and applying them to the net national income of the Canadian people we find that 57 cents out of every dollar that is earned by Canadians is taken back by governments at one level or another. If we include the net cost of government, that cost which is financed through taxes and not through other sources of income, we find that nearly 50 per cent of every dollar that is earned by Canadians is taken back by government in the form of taxes to pay for the cost of government. The taxes which I speak are taxes which are levied on net income; they are not paid out of the gross national product. They are paid out of the net earnings of the Canadian people.
It is easy to see that we face a crisis in government spending at this time. How any government can justify an increase in spending to the extent that has taken place during the last several years is something that escapes me. The unprecedented costs of government are driving our taxes and the cost of living ever higher. By increasing taxes the Minister of Finance is attempting in some small way to control the situation.
Another factor that must be considered when talking about increased government costs is the increase in welfare costs in Canada. I am thinking particularly of the prospect that medicare will be implemented in the near future. In so many words, the Minister of Finance-and his meaning is not hard to follow-says that it is not possible, considering the economy of Canada, for this country to bear the extra weight of medicare. At the same time he says that, politically, it is not possible to drop the program. I do not understand his logic. Only three of the ten provinces had shown any willingness to go ahead with medicare. Seven provinces say they do not have enough money to pay for their share of the medicare program. They imply that they would willingly see this program postponed for a long time.
Just in case the Minister of Finance thinks that I am away out in right field somewhere, may I refer to an editorial which appeared
The Budget-Mr. Thompson in the Montreal Gazette on November 30. It sums up the matter effectively in these words:
All this has been dramatically illustrated in the case of the government's medicare proposals. The government has persisted with this plan, and is persisting with it still. But there is no evidence such a plan has any overwhelming public support. The evidence, on the contrary, is that this plan, in its present form, is beyond what the country wants, as it is beyond what it can afford.
* (4:20 p.m.)
The fact is that the federal Liberals, though making medicare one of their chief promises in the last general election, came dismally to office without an over-all majority in the house. A medicare plan did not save the C.C.F. government in Saskatchewan from being voted out of office, nor did it bring it back to power in the recent election. In Quebec the provincial Liberals emphatically supported medicare, but they lost their election to a party that did not conceal its reservations about it.
All this might have given cause for the government to reconsider whether it was really being precipitated into medicare by popular propulsion. But the evidence has continued to run against the plan. When the premiers of the provinces held their own annual conference at Fredericton this summer, they exchanged many doubts and criticisms of the plan. And the federal-provincial meeting last week showed most of the provinces (including Ontario and Quebec) quite unwilling and even unable to assume at this time the burden of paying half the cost of so expensive a scheme.
How the government got started on this billion dollar spending proposition is something not yet fully explained. At last week's conference, Mr. Sharp said that the plan's cost would be equal to an increase in the personal income tax of about 12 per cent.
And we have had a 5 per cent increase in income tax in the meantime. The article continues:
This would come about at the time when Mr. Sharp is talking of raising taxes to diminish spending deficits. How many taxes can people pay? How many are they willing to pay?
Nor can it be said that the government entered into this proposition at a time when it seemed financially feasible. The warning signals were already flying when the plan was first advanced. All governments in the country were in financial trouble, and sinking deep into deficits. The need, even then, was to come to an understanding on priorities and capacities-to see what was needed most and what there was to pay for it.
The editorial states in conclusion:
It is not possible for Mr. Sharp to go before the public with two propositions: one to clamp on more taxes to cover more of its overspending, and another to launch one of the most gigantic spending schemes, involving money-finding by the provinces, as well as by Ottawa.
This is the situation in which we find ourselves at the present time, a situation which
December 7, 1967

The Budget-Mr. Thompson affects not only the poor people who pay taxes they cannot afford to pay but even bank presidents. I am sure that the reactions of the public to a speech made in Montreal by the president of the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce just three days before that editorial appeared on November 30 must have caused concern to the Minister of Finance. Referring to the taxation and financial policies of the government, Mr. Neil J. McKinnon told a conference of financial executives that a swindle had been perpetrated on the great majority of the populace who were least able to protect themselves against the consequences. Let me give an illustration of this. A man who bought a $1,000 government bond paying 4.5 per cent interest nine years ago could sell it now for no more than $790. Why? Because the price of money has been inflated, along with the price of everything else. And the $790 would not buy as much today as $600 would have done when the bond was issued to mature in 25 years. So the man who trusted his government with his life's savings has taken about a 40 per cent loss.
This is an illustration of the "massive swindle", to use Mr. McKinnon's words, which involves those least able to protect themselves.
The New Democratic party in its amendment has condemned the government for its financial policies. However, their spokesman, the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis), went on to expound the policies which he and his hon. friends believe the government should implement. What seems strange to me is that these policies are basically the same as those which have been implemented by a labour government in Britain as a result of which Britain has been brought to her knees financially, even to the point where she has been obliged to devalue the pound. And despite this drastic action her financial future for the next two or three years is far from being assured. Can hon. members not see that these financial policies being advanced as alternatives to what the government is doing are no better than those which the Minister of Finance is advocating? Surely the time has come when something different must be tried so far as economic policies are concerned.
We have wealth untold in this country, enough to meet the needs of every Canadian and more, without difficulty. It is not a problem of production; it is a problem of distribution. Money was designed and intended to be a means of distribution between producers

and consumers. After all, there is no reason to produce anything except that somebody, somewhere, wishes to consume or use it. Yet the financial policies being applied by the present government and by the government which preceded it have, along with those suggested by the New Democratic party, proved incapable of coping with the problems which face us.
The time has come when Canadians themselves have lost confidence in their economy. Some people in this country complain in anti-American tones about the effect of United States investment in Canada. I will say again, as I have on other occasions, that Americans have more confidence in Canada than have Canadians themselves when it comes to investing capital. I say this because on a per capita basis Canadians are investing $3 in the United States for every $1 which Americans are investing here.
I came across an article the other day describing the way in which business had increased on the Chicago stock exchange. The writer stated that the sharp rise in this year's trading volume was attributed largely to increased trading by Canadians. It was Canadians who had pushed up the volume of business. Our own brokerage houses confirm that Canadians are move confident in the United States economy than in their own and more willing to invest their money in United States stocks and bonds than in Canadian development. I believe this is because the policies of our governments in Canada destroy the confidence of the Canadians people in their own economy.
It is true we are comparatively few, just 20 million people. Neverthelesss, if we could only use our own credit, if we could only use our own know-how in the development of our resources, if we could only evolve our own financial policies to meet our needs, I do not think the financial situation we now face would turn out to be difficult in any way.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
I should like to refer briefly to an editorial which appeared in the Edmonton Journal of March 15 because it supports the argument I am making. It quotes Mr. George Rogers, chairman of the Canadian Economic Foundation, as saying:
Right now we are on a roller coaster, and we cannot get off. To keep prices from increasing we would have immediately to clamp a ceiling on government spending; and to reduce prices we would have to reduce total government spending by 5 per cent a year for several years.
December 7, 1967

The article continues:
No realistic person expects a reduction in government spending, but who was prepared for the almost incredible budgetary estimates tabled in the Commons Monday? They forecast a staggering increase in federal spending.
So we have a staggering deficit now facing us which has resulted in the increase in taxes that is before us at this time.
Payments to the provinces will increase by $340,000,000. Will provincial levies on the same taxpayers' pockets from which Ottawa extracts its money be reduced accordingly?
Farther on the article states:
-Mr. Louis Rasminsky, governor of the Bank of Canada, directs attention to the fact that the expenditures of provincial and municipal governments last year rose more rapidly than their revenues.
This is the pattern at all government levels, but it is the example of the federal government through its policies which is leading the provincial governments to increase their expenditures. That is why there is so much fear at the present time about the implementation of medicare. It is going to involve the expenditure of half a billion dollars on the part of the federal government and an almost similar amount on the part of the provinces. Thus we go on and on increasing the costs of government.
This article also refers to the increase in the cost of old age universal pensions and the increase in the budget of the C.B.C. It refers to other expenditures and then closes with these words:
The bill will be paid in higher taxes or higher prices through inflation-or both. Where will it all end? How many taxpayers would like the increases in total government expenditures to be not more than half the year to year increases in the gross national product?
I think most Canadians would say yes to that. This is the challenge that faces the government. Yet in the face of this challenge we find it advancing policies that do not lead to the solution of the problem. In fact they just increase the problem. This is the situation we face.
Having said this, Mr. Speaker, it would be wrong not to say something about the alternatives which I think could be implemented. For a long time Social Credit has been talking about policies, some of which have been adopted but all of which I believe one day will have to be implemented by governments in Canada.
If we are going to face up to the crisis caused by increasing government expenditures and increasing government deficits-I
The Budget-Mr. Thompson have said nothing about the increase in personal credit buying by Canadians, which has risen faster this year than in recent years-it will become imperative that money reform be implemented in a way that it is not being implemented at the present time. When governments believe that by increasing taxes they can correct inflationary trends in an economy that they describe as too hot, something is wrong with the logic of this stand because if increased taxes were the answer to the inflationary trends, in the economy today we would not have inflation inasmuch as there has been a rising pattern of increases in taxes over the years. There must be another alternative.
I believe that one of the alternatives that can be implemented is to bring in fiscal policies which will encourage Canadians to invest in their own economy. We have heard a great deal about the recommendations of the Carter report and about the necessity to introduce a capital gains tax. If succession duties were eliminated-these are forms of double taxation in themselves-it might be well to talk about the implementation of a limited capital gains tax, but we cannot have it both ways and expect to attain the objective that is our goal. Therefore rather than discouraging investment in Canadian resources, such investment must be encouraged. It is in this regard that tax reform is most necessary.
Beyond this it is necessary that we begin to use our own credit, particularly in those areas that relate to expansion of the capital development programs that are required for the services that governments must give to the Canadian economy. This again is a matter of encouragement. There is no more important need in this regard than housing. There is no reason why we cannot build houses today with money having a special category or classification which would not command the high rates of interest that commercial loans involve.

If we can provide capital in the form of soft loans to underdeveloped countries at an interest cost of three quarters of one per cent, then we should be able to provide money at 2 per cent or 3 per cent as an incentive to home production which would help expand our economy and develop our productivity.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
We must not only hold steady on government spending but we must also give an example to our economy, to our workers, to hold steady as well. It seems to me that increases in wages and prices must follow closely in line with increases in national productivity. Moreover, in an automated society wage increases must be spread beyond the narrow corridor of workers represented by trade unions in special sectors where strikes can cause a national crisis. A country cannot stand a 30 per cent increase in wages in one year without massive effects on productivity and exports. The federal government must take the lead and keep its rate of spending down to something below the rate of increase in the productivity of the nation. Wage increases must likewise be kept down to that level. Beyond that we may have some hope of maintaining a cost of living increase which will bear some relationship to the increase in the productivity of the country. If we do not do that and support it with a different financial and monetary policy in areas of public development, then we are going to go from one crisis to another.
What concerns me and those in this party at this time is simply that we are on the verge of a crisis which is going to envelop us in such a way that we will not be able to control it in the way that the minister suggests we can control it now by these limited policies. Surely we must give something better than we are giving to the people of Canada in respect of the economy of this country.

Mr. Speaker, listening to the official spokesman for the official opposition one would think that running a budget deficit was a crime, that increased government spending should be outlawed, that inflation was an indictable offence and that devaluation of a nation's currency should be punishable by death. If this was true the hon.
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Rinfret).]
member for Perth (Mr. Monteith) would not be in the house today, nor would many of the former cabinet ministers of the Conservative party. The former leader of the official opposition, once the prime minister of this country, the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), would not be here. They would all have been hanged, drawn and quartered long ago. They would have been imprisoned in the late 1950's put into solitary confinement in the early 1960's, and would all have passed on to their last reward when the devaluation of the Canadian dollar took place in those good old, bad old days of 1962.
The present leader of the Conservative party does not escape this indictment. The hon. member for Perth talked about the present Liberal government as though it was the last of the big spenders. We on this side of the house are pikers by comparison with the record of the Stanfield government of Nova Scotia. If one is talking of expenditures his record is an impressive one, indeed. speechtext:
Former premier Stanfield was not alone in his big spending habits. Conservative premiers everywhere in Canada have been heaping one government expenditure on top of another. In Ontario, for instance, provincial expenditures since the mid-1950's up to the present time have gone up four times. In premier Roblin's Manitoba they have gone up four and a half times. This only goes to show that Conservative premiers are lavish spenders. Not only that, it also shows that these provincial governments have been mainly responsible for the increase in taxes which has taken place in this country in recent years.
What do the over-all statistics show? They show, as I said before, that federal government expenditure on federal account has gone up by roughly two thirds, or 70 per cent, over the past decade. Outlays by all of the provinces taken together, meanwhile, have gone up nearly fourfold.
The provinces, it is true, have had to deal with such top priority items as education, health and municipal services, but they have dealt with them in a lavish manner. And they have frequently turned to Ottawa for help in this regard. Witness the fact that Ottawa has been turning over increasing amounts of money directly to the provinces. In the mid-1950's it was turning money over to the provinces at an annual rate of $500 million. Now five times as much money is being turned over to the provincial premiers. Some $2.5 billion will be turned over to the provincial governments in the coming year. It is more than 20 per cent of our current federal budget and it shows why it has been increasingly difficult for the federal government to budget for a surplus, in the light of these payments to the provinces, at a time when the really big spenders are the provincial premiers who have been spending money as though it were really going out of style.
Perhaps for clarification I should deal in percentages. Ten years ago Ottawa spent about 16 per cent of our gross national product on federal projects and programs of one kind of another. The corresponding figure today is down from 16 per cent. It is more like 13 per cent. The federal government, in
The Budget-Mr. Davis other words, has been taking less money proportionately out of the pockets of the Canadian taxpayers. The provinces, meanwhile have been much more ambitious. Together with the local municipalities, creatures of the provinces, they have accounted for the fact that governments collectively now spend about one third or roughly 33 per cent of our gross national product on government activities of one kind or another. Think of it. Federal expenditures on federal projects now add up to 13 per cent of our gross national product. But these are far outpaced by the spending programs of provinces, 16 per cent, and municipalities, 4 per cent. Together they make up the remaining 20 per cent. In other words, 13 per cent is spent by the federal government and 20 per cent by the provinces and their creatures, the municipalities.
Hon. members talk about deficits. Ottawa has been running a big surplus for years if we leave out the transfers to the provinces. It has been running a surplus in the order of 20 per cent. We would have a $2 billion surplus this year were it not for these payments to the provinces. It would be roughly 20 per cent of the federal government account alone.
Let me refer briefly to a comparison of the performance of the government of this country and the economy in the last ten years. Most of us know that the great depression occurred in the early 1930's when prime minister R. B. Bennett was in office. He was a Conservative so it should come as no surprise to learn that our late depression, the depression of 1957 to 1962, also occurred when a Conservative government was in power. This was the regime headed by the present hon. member for Prince Albert. It distinguished itself by running budget deficits which in absolute current dollars as well as in relative terms were the largest that this country has ever known.

A comparison between this fateful five year period and the last five years of the current Liberal administration might well be left to an independent authority, the Economic Council of Canada. Its latest annual report on current expansion since 1962 had this to say:
-this represents probably the longest, uninterrupted expansion-and certainly the longest peacetime expansion-in Canadian history.
It also had this to say:
It also constitutes the largest expansion in terms of the absolute rise in the volume of total

December 7, 1967
The Budget-Mr. Davis output and total employment. Even in terms of percentage change, the rise in industrial output was exceeded only by that occurring as the economy climbed out of the pit of the great depression.
Since the early 1960's "Canada has in fact experienced what could appropriately be described as a great expansion". Those are the words of the Economic Council of Canada. This certainly underlines the old saying that Liberal times are good times.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
I should also like to draw attention to other figures and comparisons which appear on page 12 of the latest report of the Economic Council of Canada. The report shows that our national output has grown three times as fast in the last five years as it did in the years when the hon. member for Prince Albert was in power. It shows that productivity, that is, output per man hour in industry or industrial efficiency, if you like, has grown five times as fast. It shows that unemployment has been cut in half, from 7 per cent on the average in 1962 to around 3J per cent today.
To those who are crying havoc I would also point out that our record of the last five years compares favourably even with that of the United States. The Economic Council of Canada said on page 13 of their report:
Although this great expansion was common to both Canada and the United States, its vigour was considerably more pronounced in Canada.
The opposite, unfortunately, was true in the late 1950's and early 1960's when the Conservative party was in power. So far I have been talking about big figures and round aggregates. I would like to be more specific. Annual investment in new plant and equipment fell between 1956 and 1961. Since then it has grown by more than 50 per cent. Exports have grown considerably. The hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Hees) likes to take credit for his great export drive in those fateful years leading up to 1962, but the fact is that since he left office the rate of increase in our export sales has been stepped up fourfold. The amount of foreign exchange, in other words, that we are earning from selling our goods and services to other countries has increased immensely since the Liberals came to power.
So much for the past, Mr. Speaker. Things have improved a great deal, but we have current problems. Our biggest single problem is inflation, with which we have to deal now. Granted, it is not confined to Canada alone; it is a world wide phenomenon. But we have

to learn, and learn quickly, to keep prices and wages under control. If we do not we will undermine the willingness of Canadians to save, we will hurt those people who have to live on fixed incomes and we will make the management process all the more difficult in industry and government alike.
Perhaps I should describe the situation in this way, that our economy is delicately balanced. It is balanced on a sort of knife edge, a knife edge with the abyss of unemployment on one side and the hazards of inflation on the other. Increased government spending may put more people to work but it will also add to the fires of inflation. Money wisely spent can make our economy more productive. Tax dollars spent merely to perpetuate the life of dying industries or of inefficiently operated crown corporations will cause inflation, and you can be sure of that.
The Minister of Finance, trying to operate in a free enterprise system, has several big levers which he can pull. He can expand our money supply and he can cut government expenditure. He cannot really tell business and labour what to do. From what I said earlier, the fact that federal income and expenditures now amount to only about 13 per cent of our national income illustrates that the leverage of the Minister of Finance in respect of the government's spending is less than at any time in our post-war history.
He can draw certain guide lines. If I have any criticism to make of the present government I would say it has not drawn and certainly has not published these guide lines to the extent I would like to have seen. I would like the government to indicate quite clearly what the order of magnitude of increase in prices and wages can be, what is the maximum that is tolerable in this country and what is the maximum that is consistent with a modest degree of inflation in Canada.
I would like to think that a guide line would be drawn tolerating an increase, if you like, a maximum increase, in prices and wages of the order of 5 per cent per year. We have had in recent years an increase in productivity of the order of 3 per cent. It has been slipping toward 2 per cent. If we have increases in wages and prices in excess of 2 or 3 per cent a year we have some degree of inflation. If we have wage and price increases of the order of 7 per cent or 8 per cent a year, as recent wage agreements, particularly in the larger industries and negotiated by the more powerful unions would indicate, then we are in for a substantial

The Budget-Mr. Davis number of miles flown, the number of passengers carried and the amount of freight carried were almost identical in the case of both companies in 1966. It is interesting to note that Air Canada, which is more of a monopoly than is Northwest Orient Airlines, had a higher load factor. It has a load factor of 65 per cent while Northwest Orient Airlines had only 55 per cent. Each aircraft had more seats filled in Air Canada's case.
I think we will all admit that Air Canada is excellent in the air. It has first class equipment and its safety record is second to none. This is borne out by the financial statistics. Both of these corporations spend about 20 per cent of their total revenue on what might loosely be called their flying operations. But there the similarity ends. Air Canada's traffic servicing, most of the Canadian travelling public will agree, leaves something to be desired. Still, Air Canada spent 14.3 per cent of its income on air traffic servicing while Northwest Orient Airlines spent only 9.4 per cent. Air Canada is a virtual monopoly. Northwest Orient Airlines, on the other hand, has to compete flat out with a number of other carriers in the United States. Nevertheless Air Canada spent 15.4 per cent of its revenue into sales promotion, exactly double Northwest Orient's 7.7 per cent in 1966. When it comes to general administration we see much the same thing. The figure for Air Canada last year was 3.9 per cent while that for Northwest Orient Airlines was 2.4 per cent.
There is another item in respect of Air Canada which bears careful examination. I note that the maintenance figure for Air Canada was 19.5 per cent, more than double Northwest Orient Airlines figure of 9.5 per cent. Why is this? I am told this is due to the servicing of a number of older Viscount aircraft, many of which will be taken out of service by 1970 or 1971. But the real answer is that Air Canada insists on carrying on a number of regional operations in this country. It is ont only in the big jet business but also in the smaller, regional carrier business as well. If Air Canada were to back out of this latter field and leave it to private enterprise I am sure that the subsidies required from the federal government would be much smaller than the losses incurred by Air Canada in carrying on this particular type of activity.
The real clincher, I think, is employment. Air Canada employs far more people than does Northwest Orient Airlines. In 1966 it had 13,718 employees. Northwest Orient Air-

lines, flying roughly the same number of people over roughly the same number of miles and carrying a similar volume of air traffic, employed 8,875 people. Our crown owned corporation, in other words, employed roughly 50 per cent more people to do a similar job in the air for Canadians.
Now I will refer to taxation. Air Canada paid to the federal government taxes of the order of $3 million in 1956. Northwest Orient Airlines, on the other hand, shouldered a tax burden of more than $46 million. In other words, last year the private company was yielding a tax payment to the United States economy of $46 million.
Last Thursday night when the Minister of Finance submitted his budget, I was glad to hear that Air Canada would be forced to go out into the money market in order to raise funds of its own. It will at least have to show how it expects to be able to pay interest on its bonds and have something to spare. In this way it will be brought into much closer contact with the business community. It will have to compete with other well managed industries for its funds. This is all to the good.
I should like to turn very briefly to another corporation, namely, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. This year the C.B.C. will be receiving $140 million from the federal treasury. In addition it will be earning, over and above that figure, at least $25 million in the form of revenue for advertisements shown on its television system or broadcast by radio. Let us compare this with the $14 million budget of the privately owned C.T.V. One is more than ten times the other. I understand that C.T.V. now reaches approximately 70 per cent of the Canadian viewing public. If I were to double its $14 million expenditure to allow for the fact that it does not reach into many homes in Quebec and other French speaking areas, and double it again to allow for it to reach into a number of outlying areas in the rest of the country which are not commercially attractive to private enterprise, the figure would still only be $56 million. Even this does not bear a favourable comparison with the very large figure for the C.B.C.
