Mr. Speaker, in speaking in support of the amendment my remarks will centre around two words which appear in it, namely, the
December 7, 1967

"vacillation" and "extravagance" of the government. Within the committee framework of parliament we have had for many years a public accounts committee which has been charged with the responsibility of dealing with the Auditor General's report and with other financial matters which come to the attention of the house and are referred to this committee. I do not think that any committee of the house has been more diligent in bringing to the attention of the ministers and the house the waste and the extravagance which they have uncovered in the course of their work.
Last year the committee met very regularly. Unfortunately this has not been the case this year. Let me point out the government's vacillation in this regard. Last January 9 the report of the Auditor General for 1966 was tabled in the house and, mark you, Mr. Speaker, on April 5, three months later, this committee received its terms of reference from the house. Three months were wasted there. Immediately after the committee received its terms of reference it met, on April 13, and continued to meet until the house closed on April 26.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
The house opened again on May 8. On May 19, under standing order 65, the committees of the house were set up. However, an organization meeting of the public accounts committee has not been called by the government. I believe there is no justification for this delay, no justification for the lack of interest in grappling with the nation's economic situation and dealing with matters that this servant of parliament, the Auditor General, has brought before it by means of his report. The government has ignored this committee and has not set it up.
Over the years this committee has dealt with various forms of waste and extravagance in government operations. The other day I read an editorial and it led me to think how wonderful it would be if we could have the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Greene) as a member of the public accounts committee. The minister was attending an FAO meeting in Rome at which the representatives were discussing the operating costs of FAO. Of the total of $60 million contributed to this organization Canada contributes 4.1 per cent. There was a discussion of staff increases which since 1957 have amounted to 300 per cent. The minister had this to say:
If they lose faith-
The Budget-Mr. Hales
He was referring to the countries contributing to this organization.
-these Canadian taxpayers, in the efficiency of our endeavours, if they come to believe that their taxes are but adding to the bureaucracy or to the pile of papers in some mirky vault, they will lose the will to participate.
This is what our minister said in Rome, and if he would just bring those words back to Canada they would make an excellent prescription for Ottawa. During his remarks in Rome he also said:
New funds are hard to come by and a dollar saved is a dollar earned.
Wouldn't he make a wonderful member of the public accounts committee? I hope he will instil some of these principles of thrift and saving into the cabinet of which he is a member. There was an editorial by Fraser Robertson in the Globe and Mail for December 1 headed "M.P.'s Also Responsible For Final Decision". He was referring to this terrible budget. I resent that statement because I feel that members of parliament have been sincere in bringing to the attention of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) the great perils and troubles of our economic situation. The public accounts committee, which represents parliament as a whole on public spending, when called into session, has been very diligent in its work.
Let us look for a few minutes at some of the recommendations made by the public accounts committee and what has been done about them. In the fourth report for 1963 the committee pointed out that the Unemployment Assistance Act was inadequate and that there were certain deficiencies in the shareable costs. However, there has been no action taken and there has been vacillation in this regard. The government introduced the Canada Assistance Plan, but it was not incorporated into the unemployment assistance scheme.
In the fourth report of the committee for 1964 there is a reference to the findings of the Glassco commission. At that time, out of the original 276 recommendations the committee found that there were 151 recommendations which had not been acted upon. If all these recommendations had been put into operation they certainly would have yielded substantial savings. I will give the government its due by saying they have implemented some recommendations since that committee report, but there are still many Glassco commission recommendations left outstanding.

December 7, 1967
The Budget-Mr. Hales
The Auditor General had this to say concerning the Glassco commission, and I quote from page 3 of his report for 1966:
Meanwhile, administrative overhead in departments and agencies continues to rise substantially in terms of staff needs and office costs. I advised the house last year that when this royal commission concluded its work in 1962-63, administrative overhead in terms of staff needs and office costs was to the order of $1,000 million. The comparable figure presently estimated for 1966-67 is $1,325 million, an increase of over 30 per cent during the past four years.
The Auditor General's report was presented to the government but we have seen no action and, if anything, there has been an increase in the above figures.
In so far as crown corporations are concerned, the public accounts committee made some recommendations. The crown corporations spend billions of dollars of the taxpayers' money, but no member of their boards of directors reports directly to parliament on their operations. We do not even have the Auditor General as the auditor for seven of these large corporations. I think we should at least have a representative when we realize how much money these corporations spend.
The crown corporations whose books the Auditor General does not audit are Air Canada, the Bank of Canada, Canadian National Railways, C.N. Security Trust, Canadian Wheat Board, the C.B.C. and the Industrial Development Bank. If the government does not feel the Auditor General should be the auditor, as the committee suggested, perhaps he could be co-auditor. Perhaps, on the other hand, the government would adopt the suggestion of the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Walker) who had a private bill that was of great interest which would provide for one member of parliament being on the board of each crown corporation.
I should like to turn to some other recommendations the committee made which it was believed would at least prevent government extravagance and waste. There was a suggestion concerning the form of the estimates. The committee asked for a brief note to be included setting out the increases in the size of staffs of departments and crown corporations. In this way members would know which departments had increased in size. The Glassco commission made a very thorough study of the C.B.C. but the officials of that organization have ignored that report. It has been brought to the attention of this house but nothing has been done. Reference was made also to Governor General's warrants which are used when money is required and
[Mr. Hales.l
parliament is not in session. It is hardly necessary to list examples; they are all in the Auditor General's report.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
Another recommendation that was made in 1964 was the institution of an accounts receivable system. Imagine a business as large as the government operating without an accounts receivable system, Mr. Speaker. What happens under such a system is that departments of government have a control figure to which is added the amount they have charged. The moneys then paid on account are deducted and the balance should correspond to the control figure. But during the course of our studies we discovered many departments had no accounts receivable control. Though some improvements have been made in this direction there are still many departments without any accounts receivable control system.
In its seventh report in 1964 the committee expressed great concern over the way inventories were being kept in the Department of National Defence. This department kept only a physical inventory, not one that itemized cost as well. The department knew how many items it had but not their cost. Imagine running a business in this way, Mr. Speaker, where the inventory consists of a physical count with no disclosure of cost or what it costs to carry the inventory. When equipment is turned over to Crown Assets for disposal a cost figure is required so as to set a resale figure. The recommendation of the committee would have prevented waste and extravagance but to my knowledge no action has yet been taken.
In our eighth report in 1964 we dealt with the subject of general election expenses. We asked the government to amend the Canada Elections Act so that any advance poll which had had 15 or less voters could be crossed off the list and would not have to be set up at the next election. But they did not do so. The result was that during the last election the chief electoral officer had to continue to operate these advance polls. It is startling to note that in the 1965 election there were 371 such polls with less than 15 votes, 16 polls with no votes, 20 with less than one vote and 20 polls with less than 2 votes. In all there were 427 polls which could have been struck off the list and taken out of operation. I inquired from the chief electoral officer what was the average cost of a poll and was informed that it was $136. This means that Canada wasted $58,072 simply because the government failed

51G5
to pass an order in council to correct a situation that was brought to their attention by the public accounts committee. This is the sort of thing that indicates a lack of interest or sincerity and in addition costs the taxpayers a lot of money.

subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I think what the hon. member wants to know is when the act was last considered. When the Conservative party was in office it brought in the new act, but this is no excuse for the present government not passing an order in council to change the regulations. I understand it is possible under the act to pass an order in council to change the regulations, but this has never been done. Therefore, during the last election all of these advance polls to which I have referred were put into operation even though they were useless, unnecessary and costly. I hope that such an order in council will be put into effect before the next election.
Another waste of the taxpayers money occurred in the Department of Trade and Commerce. The Department of Trade and Commerce administers the Gas Inspection Act, the Electricity Inspection Act and the Weights and Measures Act, and these statutes provide for the imposition of fees to meet the cost of operation. In 1965 the committee reported that the department was losing money and for the year ended March, 1966 the cost of administration exceeded revenue by $735,000. This loss included salaries and expenses of district offices, but, Mr. Speaker, if we add to that the cost of labs, branch administration and services from other departments the loss jumps to $1,710,000. Nothing has been done to correct this situation. It is a question of raising rates for these services that are rendered by the Department of Trade and Commerce. There is much talk of the shortage of houses. The government contends that it has insufficient money to lend so that the houses that are needed in Canada may be built. This sum of $1,710,000
The Budget-Mr. Hales could build 120 homes each costing $15,000. I suggest this is an area where savings should be made.
The committee also made some recommendations in connection with revenues of the St. Lawrence seaway meeting expenses, but no action has been taken on them.
In the fourth report of the committee in 1966 the savings bank division of the Post Office Department was dealt with. There are about 300,000 accounts in this division, 200,000 of which are classified as dormant or unclaimed. The interest on these accounts amounted to $67,000 for the year ended March 31, 1966. The committee recommended that these unclaimed balances should be dealt with in the same way as the chartered banks handle them, but nothing has been done. This $67,000 lies dormant. These amounts should revert to the crown. Another five homes could have been built with the interest alone.
I could give all sorts of examples, Mr. Speaker, of the money that is wasted by the Department of Transport, particularly in the matter of ship repair. There was one case where the tender amounted to $43,346 but by the time the ship was finished the cost had risen to $130,851. The committee recommended that when extras were involved they should be handled on a cost plus basis, the profit to be limited to the percentage of profit realized on the original contract price. The entire contract should be subject to cost audit by government auditors.
Take the case of the Bonaventure, Mr. Speaker. We all know how much it cost to put that vessel in order, some $12 million. The committee also reported on the cost of abandoned design plans for a ferry vessel. Some $120,000 was paid to the architects although the Department of Transport and the C.N.R. never got together to discuss the plans. Before calling on the architects to draw plans they could not make up their minds whether the vessel was to be a full icebreaker or an ice-strengthened ship. As the result a loss of $120,000 was incurred. With that amount of money the government could have built eight homes at $15,000 each.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
Another $55,000 went down the drain because the architects were told, after plans had been drawn for a ferry, that the Canadian National wanted provisions for extra rail car weights. Apparently this had not been included in the original plans. We recommended that basic data be completely verified before placing any request in the

December 7, 1967
The Budget-Mr. Hales hands of an architect. This is another example of how the government has brought about waste through its extravagances and failures. I could cite many other instances but I shall not take the time of the house to do so.
I spoke about crown corporations. The report of the Auditor General to parliament speaks of the many wastes and extravagances through which the taxpayers' money dwindles away.
I wish to say something briefly about the travelling expenses which this government has incurred. I have compared the travelling expenses of all departments of government for the year 1966-67 with those for 1967-68. In one year-mark this, Mr. Speaker-there has been an increase of over $18 million in travelling expenses for all departments of government. Yes, in one year. If we look at the various departments we see that travelling expenses for the Department of External Affairs increased by $833,000, the Department of National Health and Welfare showed an increase in travelling expenses of $830,000, the Department of Transport showed an increase of $965,000, and the Department of National Defence showed an increase of $9,439,000 in one year. If we average the total figure out among all the civil servants in all departments-one should include here every person, from the man who sweeps the floor to the deputy minister at the top-we find that approximately $400 per person was spent for travelling expenses in 1967-68.
What control have we over such travelling expenses? Is this government to go on permitting this sort of thing? Are we to have civil servants flitting all over the country, with one here, one there and two turning up in the same place where only one is needed to do a job? Is there to be no control over travelling expenses? Apparently all that civil servants must do is to put in a requisition and it will be paid. It is high time that the government looked into the travelling expenses that are being incurred especially when in one year they increased by approximately $18 million. I wanted to speak about increases incurred by other departments, but I see that I do not have enough time to do so.
I wish to spend some time talking about government surplus materials which are sold by Crown Assets Disposal Corporation. The worst offender in this regard is the Department of National Defence which divides the materials that are to be sold by Crown Assets into two categories. One category is "surplus but serviceable". In other words, this is

another way of saying that the government bought too much of such material. The loss in 1966, in round figures, for such materials was $52 million. That figure is the difference between what the government paid for such materials and what it sold them for. The second category is "obsolete but serviceable". In that category the government incurred a $48 million loss. In round figures, for both categories the government incurred a loss of about $100 million. That amount of money could have built about 6,700 homes at $15,000 each, which are so badly needed.
I wanted to deal with some other government departments, such as the Department of Justice, the Department of Manpower and Immigration, the Department of Labour and the Department of Industry. I shall have time to deal only with the Department of Industry.
We all recall the debate on the bill which set up the Department of Industry. We in the opposition argued that the Department of Trade and Commerce could do anything that the Department of Industry was set up to do. But, oh no. We were told that by taking staff from the Departments of Trade and Commerce and Defence Production and putting them into the Department of Industry there would be hardly any increase in staff requirements. Consequently, when the Department of Industry was set up in 1963-64 it employed 274 people. The estimates for 196768 show that 783 people will be required for that department, an increase of 509 people or roughly 200 per cent. The Department of Defence Production in 1963-64 employed 1,699 people. The estimate for 1967-68 is that 3,684 people are to be employed. That is an increase of 1,985 people, or more than 100 per cent. The same picture holds true for the Department of Trade and Commerce. That department has added 298 persons to its staff, which is a 60 per cent increase. I could run through most of the departments this way and show that this government has been wasteful and extravagant all along the line.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, the illustrations such as I have given have been given by others over a considerable period of time. What I have said is not new; it has been said by every reputable financial writer and newspaperman in Canada for the past six months. People have lost confidence in this government. We have an outflow of millions of dollars from this country on the part of Canadians who are selling Canadian securities and purchasing United States securities. This
December 7, 1967

is shocking but it has been going on for some time. People have done this because they say that at least they lose their money through inflation in the United States only half as fast as they are currently losing it in Canada, and there are some other advantages.
I wish to conclude, Mr. Speaker, by quoting again the remarks of the Minister of Agriculture. He said:
If they lose faith, these Canadian taxpayers, in the efficiency of our endeavors, if they come to believe that their taxes are but adding to the bureaucracy, or to the pile of papers in some murky vault, they will lose the will to participate.
I have not lost my confidence in Canada, Mr. Speaker, but I have lost confidence completely in this government and I propose to vote for the amendment.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak in support of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Monteith) in the hope that I may be able to assist in convincing hon. members that it is their patriotic duty to defeat this government and rid the country of an administration which has been notably inept in its handling of Canadian affairs.
Listening to the budget speech of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) I came to the conclusion that one of the most revealing statements contained in it, the statement which has the most far reaching effect, was the admission that it is almost impossible for the government to make any sizeable reduction in its budget. The minister explained how difficult it is to cut back federal spending. He had this to say as reported on page 4903 of Hansard:
We make a large number of substantial transfer payments to the provinces and municipalities such as equalization payments, hospital insurance, aid for education and the Canada assistance social welfare plan, most of which increase automatically under statute or agreement with the province.
We have in addition . . . major programs consisting of transfer payments to persons, including family and youth allowances, veterans' pensions and adult training allowances. All of these are also fixed mainly by population factors and by statute.
In other words, this government is not the captain of its own ship. It is bound by statutes and arrangements which have been made in the past to continue to budget at a very high level.

speechtext:
I think the Minister of Finance had ample opportunity to put forward his point of view and I would appreciate being able to put forward my point of view without getting into a lighthearted debate with the minister. I know he is very glib when it comes to putting forward questions but I would appreciate being able to continue my own remarks at this time.
Is it any wonder people think that the government's ship is floundering on the sea of ministerial irresponsibility? The minister went on to say that more than half of the anticipated increase in the budget was attributable to the type of uncontrollable expenditure he had described.
The point I am trying to make is that the government has lost control over a very large proportion of its budget, the portion which involves items which are fixed by statute or which represent programs of a continuing nature. This and future governments are committed to continue making expenditures on at least the present scale simply because hon. gentlemen opposite have bound themselves and all future governments to continue existing expenditures permanently.

subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The government must bear responsibility for the unwarranted increase in the budget during its term of office. The argument put forward by the minister that federal expenditures accounted for only 16.8 per cent of the gross national product compared with 19.2 per cent in the fiscal year 1961-62 is entirely unacceptable. Similarly, there is no justification for rationalizing the federal budget by indications that provincial governments and municipalities spend more than Ottawa does. This is a facetious argument and it should not have been put forward.
I read an interesting article in the Financial Post of December 2, written by J. Harvey Perry, the executive director of the Canadian Bankers' Association who, incidentally, was a member of the Carter commission on taxation. He wrote:
One of the recommendations which the Carter Commission nearly made, but didn't, is that one of the very earliest exercises in reviewing existing programs should be in the area of social welfare.
I believe that in one of our drafts we had included such a recommendation but later we decided it was none of our business. However, if any part
5168	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Ballard of our present governmental financial structure comes even close to competing with the tax system for being unplanned, ramshackle and jerry-built, it is social welfare. Welfare is the No. 1 subject, following taxation, requiring an immediate and complete overhaul.
I must say in all honesty that I believe the Minister of Finance has exerted pressure in an effort to have the government take a new look at social welfare. This is long overdue, and Canadians outside the party which forms the government are placing a great deal of reliance on the minister in this connection.
The hon. gentleman brags, as reported at page 4902 of Hansard, that since this government came to office it has been "putting into place the major reforms required to complete Canada's social security system." I am pleased the minister acknowledges that the government has accepted responsibility for increasing Canada's budget from some $7 billion in 1963 to $11 billion in 1967. It will surely go down in history as being Canada's most spendthrift government.

subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In addition to the huge
expenditures already reported, and even in the face of the dire financial and economic situation with which this country is confronted, the government is committed to add yet another welfare scheme to the list, medicare, which it is estimated will add a minimum of $600 million a year to the federal budget and a similar amount to the budgets of the provinces. This is a glaring example of irresponsibility. Faced with a future fraught with economic uncertainty, hon. members opposite are adding another welfare scheme costing well over a billion dollars a year to what Mr. Perry calls an unplanned, ramshackle and jerry-built social welfare system.
The prospect of piling more taxes on the shoulders of already overburdened taxpayers in order to finance the proposed medicare scheme has brought protests from a large number of people and on their behalf I beseech the minister to use his influence on the government to postpone the implementation of medicare. I might say I have received letters on this subject from a number of people and organizations, including the Calgary chamber of commerce, protesting vehemently against the implementation of this scheme. In a letter to the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) from the Canadian Chamber of

DEBATES	December 7, 1967
Commerce, dated November 17, the following paragraph appears:
The delegates at the Canadian Chamber's recent annual meeting voted in favour of a policy statement supporting the provision of finacnial assistance for medical care for those who need it, and, at the same time, unanimously opposed the introduction of the universal compulsory medical care program.
The Calgary chamber of commerce also wrote a letter to the Prime Minister under date of December 4, 1967, part of which reads as follows:
The executive council of the Calgary Chamber of Commerce has unanimously endorsed the stand taken by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce in urging the federal government to arrange for an indefinite moratorium on the introduction of a universal compulsory medical care program.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
I could quote from numerous letters and editorials in support of this plea for postponement of medicare, but surely the minister is aware of the disillusionment among the public over the prospect of yet another increase in taxes. I think it must be evident to the minister and to the other members of the government that there is great concern, not only in the ranks of provincial leaders but among the general public as well, over the implementation of medicare at this time. A postponement, I suggest, would be the most prudent step for the government, considering the present economic situation in the country.
Glancing through the Montreal Gazette of November 30 I noticed that the column written by Mr. John Meyer had this headline, "Never a Federal Budget Less Fortuitous In Timing." I planned to read that column but before doing so my attention was drawn to the headline over the column next to it, "New Plan Would Cut United States Deficit $11 Bln." It revealed an unusual situation. The most prosperous country in the world is planning to cut its budget by $11 billion through two different methods. One is to increase taxes and the other, surprisingly enough, and this should commend itself to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp), is to cut $4 billion from its spending in the current fiscal year.
This could be the theme for a comic opera, with the richest country in the world intending to cut its spending estimates while its next door neighbour, faced with inflation, gives no thought to cutting expenses in the current year but can only suggest an increase in taxes as a solution to its problems.
December 7, 1967	COMMONS
I think it is worth while to quote a portion of Mr. Meyer's column because it is indicative of the feeling across Canada in connection with this budget. It reads in part as follows:
It's difficult to imagine the timing for the budget being less fortuitous than it is. The economy has lost way and is wallowing in the cross-currents of indecision.
I do not know whether he meant the economy or the government when he wrote about indecision.
The public mood is one of weary resentment of government fumbling. The budget itself can offer nothing to inspire. It is, after all, hardly more than the belated correction of a gross miscalculation, or rather a series of gross miscalculations, over the past two years.
Farther on he wrote:
If Mr. Sharp is to be criticized, it should be for failing to have persuaded his colleagues in cabinet before now to the dangers of excessive spending.
This is why we on this side of the house are critical of the actions taken by the Minister of Finance. He is not fulfilling his responsibilities as the minister charged with jurisdiction over the Department of Finance.
Now I want to say just a word in connection with the planning of future expenditures by this or, in fact, by any government. I believe that in government circles it is just as necessary to plan future expenditures as it is in private industry. The government should set up a committee of the house to study the different problems and the necessity of spending for the future, for 10, 25 or 50 years ahead. This committee should assign an order of priorities to the different areas of spending. It should also be charged with the determination of the source of funds to finance future spending. It is not good enough for the government to work out a theory of spending on something it considers necessary, such as medicare, without giving any thought to how much it is going to cost and where the money is to come from.
Medicare is a good example. The minister in charge has said it will cost $600 million in the first year, but I contend members of the government do not know whether it is going to cost $600 million or a much higher figure. At the time the legislation was introduced they had no idea whence the money would come to pay the bill. That is one of the reasons we are in a mess today. It is one of the reasons we are going to be faced with increased income taxes six months from now to cover this unplanned increase in government expenditure.

The committee of which I speak should also be charged with the responsibility of allocating tax revenues between the various levels of government in order to undertake the priorities that are determined by the proper level of government. Priorities are necessary to cover such items as housing, public housing, assistance to the home owner through N.H.A. mortgages, government participation in urban transportation, social welfare plans, and government assistance from the various levels toward the control of pollution-air pollution, water and soil pollution. The committee should also assign a priority to water supplies and to the problem of waste disposal, both domestic and industrial.
One of the things I have mentioned in this list of priorities is urban transportation. It is entirely unacceptable for the government to sit idly by, realizing that 80 per cent of the people of Canada will live in urban areas by 1980. At the present time over 70 per cent live in urban areas.
The Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities has made representations to the federal government in this connection. In their report in January this year on urban transportation they said:
The requirements of the multiplying numbers of the urban population for educational services, welfare services, hospitals, roads, water and sanitary facilities, etc., have placed a severe financial strain upon the principal source of municipal revenues- the tax on real property.
I might say that the government appeared to give some credence to the plea of the municipalities for help from senior levels of government, because when the Prime Minister was speaking in Calgary on March 29 of this year he said that "there is also a growing body of opinion that federal aid can no longer most effectively play its role in community development" without providing "transportation corridors in future environmental development."
The chairman of the Winnipeg committee on streets and transit has said:
There has to be a review and a realignment of the priorities by all levels of government,... that money should be spent on problems where people are, and certainly one of the basic necessities in urban growth and development is a healthy, efficient, public transportation system.

In this connection, I would cite the great changes in the administration of our affairs which were not only facilitated but actually pressed on the government by the public service and in this regard I refer you to my speech to the house on October 10 last. No greater revolution in administration anywhere in,the world has taken place than in our public service in the past five years.
We in Canada are the most fortunate people in the world. Let us realize this and look upon my remarks which follow in a vein similar to that of a large business which must from time to time reflect and review its prospects. As anyone in business knows, we must from time to time review our priorities and readjust our spending plans to live within our revenue. We must make hard decisions in order that in the long run our business may prosper. When the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) introduced his supplementary budget proposals last week, he indicated that I would follow up on his remarks relating to expenditures and provide the house with further details as to the efforts the government has been making to restrain its planned expenditures for 1968-69 within a prescribed ceiling.

The Minister of Finance has already stated the specific goal which the government has

The Budget-Mr. Benson set for itself in the fiscal year 1968-69 which is to contain over-all budgetary expenditures in 1968-69 within a ceiling of $10.3 billion, exclusive of expenditures for medicare, and for the writing-off of the Expo deficit.

For the public service, exclusive of crown corporations, the growth in the size of the approved establishment for 1968-69, that is to say the number of positions authorized which is larger than the number actually filled at any one time, will not be allowed to rise by more than 5,000 above the numbers now
5172	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Benson authorized for the current fiscal year. This amounts to a growth rate for the public service proper of approximately 2 per cent in fiscal year 1968-69, compared to a rate of 4 per cent or more in recent years.
I might mention, in passing, that the annual increase in the post office alone, in order to keep pace with population growth and work load, is inevitably 2,000 or more annually as shown by the actual experience of recent years. I mention this fact so that hon. members may see more clearly the significance of the limitations on growth that are now proposed for 1968-69. The 5,000 limit to which I have made reference will have to include the increased numbers required for the maintenance of adequate postal services, as well as the requirements of all other departments and agencies. This means that, if the added staff requirements of the Post Office Department alone in 1968-69 are 2,000 or more, and this is a fact, then 2,000 of the additional 5,000 positions to be made available will have to be reserved for the Post Office Department leaving 3,000 positions to provide for the growth requirements of the other 25 departments and the 40 or more agencies, boards, bureaus, commissions and offices which together make up what we call the public service of Canada charged with administering the activities that parliament has assigned to them.
I should also mention that, in addition to limiting the growth of the public service in 1968-69 to 5,000 additional positions, it is also the government's intention to set a limit of 95 per cent on the number of positions within the approved establishment which can be occupied at any one time. This limitation will provide an additional salutary restraint on growth, and will, in particular, highlight those individual departments and agencies in which the pressures against the 95 per cent limitation suggest the need for a re-examination of the staff requirement and work load, well in advance of the point in time when the approved establishment is completely filled and the agency or department clamouring for additional positions.
A third element in the government's plan for limitations on staff growth is, I think, also worthy of mention. Examination of a representative number of departmental establishments has revealed that, in a significant number of instances, departments have had additions approved to their establishment and have subsequently experienced inordinate delays in filling these approved positions. Whenever positions which have

DEBATES	December 7, 1967
been authorized as necessary at a given point in time remain unfilled for six months after they have been authorized, the question is bound to arise as to how the departments have managed to get along in the interval, and whether the authorized positions continue to be necessary or even whether they were necessary in the first place. Without endeavouring to pre-judge the issue, I believe that there is justification for saying that in many instances where positions remain unfilled continuously for six months or more after they have been created they should be cancelled.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that the three steps which I have outlined for controlling the future growth of the public service will serve to demonstrate that the government seriously intends to contain within reasonable and prudent limits this important element of expenditure within its total budget for 196869. The civil payroll, exclusive of the uniformed forces and the R.C.M.P. amounts to about $1.5 billion in a total budget of $10 billion, approximately 15 per cent of the total expenditure budget. It goes without saying, therefore, that success in controlling total budgetary expenditure, depends in a very important degree on success in controlling civil payroll costs, and this in turn depends in large part on success in controlling the size of, and the growth rate in the civil establishment. I can assure the house that the government has every intention of achieving in this regard the objectives which it has set for itself. If, in the course of the year, a department or agency finds it necessary for any reason to request an increase In its establishment, it will be required to undertake a full review of its present position and to satisfy the Treasury Board that it has exhausted all possibilities of meeting the added requirement from the resources already available to it. Only when that condition has been satisfied will the Treasury Board consider a request for any additional positions. I do not think, however, that we should go so far as to impose an arbitrary absolute "freeze" on present establishments. We have examined this suggestion which has been put forward from a number of quarters. Governments in the past, both federal and provincial, have attempted to "freeze" establishments. Such efforts have never been successful. They have produced inequities, distortions, frustrations, and even waste, as senior officials have been obliged to get along without the supporting staff which they require in order to
December 7, 1967	COMMONS
function effectively. The adverse consequences of an absolute freeze persist long after the freeze itself has been abolished or has been eroded away. At the very best, a freeze succeeds only in buying time until a proper policy for restraining staff growth can be devised. A freeze is not in itself a policy: instead it is evidence that no policy exists and that the authority imposing the freeze has proven to be incapable of devising a policy. We have a policy and we are going to apply it.

Before leaving the subject of staff growth and the size of the public service, let me emphasize again a point to which the Minister of Finance referred in his speech last week, when he opened this debate. Contrary to the beliefs of many who think that the federal public service has grown abnormally over the years, statistics show that the growth of the service has remained remarkably constant in relation to population growth over the period of the last 15 years. Federal departmental employment as a percentage of the total population of Canada-the public it serves-has varied only between the extremes of 1.06 per cent and 1.17 per cent over the years 1952 and 1966 inclusive. I turn now, Mr. Speaker, to the undertaking given by the Minister of Finance -that we will contain the budgetary expenditures for 1968-69, apart from medicare and Expo deficit, within the ceiling of $10.3 billion. There have been many demands from the opposition side of the house and from other quarters during recent weeks and months that the government reveal full details as to what cuts it is making and how it intends to achieve the containment of its over-all budgetary expenditures within this $10.3 billion ceiling.
It would not, of course, be appropriate for me at this juncture, in advance of the tabling of the main estimates for 1968-69 early in the next session of parliament, to launch a debate on the government's expenditure plans for the next fiscal year. This debate cannot be properly joined until the estimates for 196869 have been tabled and the details are available for all to examine.
Despite the foregoing, I think I can give to the house sufficient details as to the over-all dimensions of the problem that we have faced in recent weeks, and as to the expenditure cuts already decided in departmental proposals and plans for 1968-69 to satisfy hon. members that we have tackled this difficult undertaking resolutely and successfully.
As hon. members know, the estimates procedure for 1968-69 really got under way in April of this year when departments and agencies were asked to submit, by the end of May, their program reviews and forecasts of probable financial requirements, not only for the balance of the current fiscal year, but also, for 1968-69, and for the three years following. When these forecasts were received and analyzed in June of this year, they showed a prospective requirement for 1968-69, if all forecast departmental requirements were to be met, of $11,500 million. This was some $1,800 million higher than the total expenditure forecast in the budget speech of the Minister of Finance of June 1, 1967, for the current fiscal year.
In August, a decision was made to establish an over-all expenditure target of $10.3 billion apart from medicare and the Expo deficit which, it was felt, should both be dealt with outside the normal budgetary target, based on year to year comparisons of normally continuing programs.
The decision as to the over-all target of $10.3 billion led in turn to the establishment of individual departmental targets of expenditure. Each department and agency was

From 1955 to 1965 Canada has had the lowest rate of productivity increase among 15 nations, including Great Britain, which has experienced serious difficulty. Our productivity has grown at the rate of only 2 per cent per capita per annum. The inflated figures the government uses are related to the birth rate, and surely the minister of revenue (Mr. Benson) is not by himself going to take credit for that, as well.
Let me quote from the first report of the economic council which in part states:

We have not been going forward in respect of productivity; we have been going backwards. Tonight the minister has chosen from two alternatives, namely increasing the productivity of this nation so we can afford to do those things that are right, just and necessary, or going along with a slothful attitude, such as his government has been displaying

in cutting its expenses to suit productivity. I suggest that the choice of increasing the productivity is the one that should have been made. How much more desirable would it be for this approach to be taken than the picayune approach the government has taken tonight?
Our society requires that we have priorities. We do not argue that a nation can have everything it wants, all at once. It should also be obvious that priorities should not only be set in respect of the public sector, but should be set also in respect of the private sector. No one can do everyting he wishes, but why should it always be the public sector which pays for the foolishness of the private sector -and there is foolishness.
Let us look at some of the so-called priorities the market system has imposed upon the Canadian public. In that year the economy spent $328 million in capital expenditures for banks and financial institutions in this country, a country which has more banks per capita than anywhere else in the world. It is significant that we spent half that amount, or $164 million, on universities. In that year we spent $351 million to build stores, shopping centres and service stations. We spent almost half of that, $188 millions, on hospitals. This is a fine sense of priorities, when we find that the construction of stores, supermarkets, bank buildings and service stations is more important than the construction of hospitals and universities. In the year 1963 we spent $399 million on industrial construction. In that same year we spent $616 million on commercial construction. Let me ask the hon. member who has just spoken which is more important, and how these priorities stack up in his view as to what is needed in this country?
Let me quote some statistics in respect of reducing government spending. These statistics are from the Economic Council of Canada. From 1961 to 1966 the total volume of final demand increased by 33 per cent; new machinery and equipment increased by four fifths and new residential construction increased by almost one half. In that same period the number of houses constructed increased by only one fifth, yet the volume of government expenditures on goods and services increased by one quarter. No one can say that housing, or services the government has provided, have increased at a faster rate
DEBATES	5187
The Budget-Mr. Saltsman than other expenditures in our economy. The contrary is true. We have spent much less for public services and housing than the wealth of our society would indicate was possible.
The central issue facing us today does not involve a question of priorities alone, but rather who it is that sets these priorities. Does the government of Canada set the priorities, or does it bow to the few financiers of this nation who demand sacrifices from the government in the way of cutting expenditures, whether they are necessary or not? Is the government helpless in the face of this type of demand? Perhaps the government's response to the old phrase "Put your house in order" means, when translated, "We do not want public expenditure"
Much of the present inflationary pressure is psychological. The financiers in this country are doing all they can to persuade Canadians that the only way to restore confidence is by cutting public expenditures. There is no consideration of the curtailment of our own demands. This is a delightful arrangement from their standpoint, and the tune has not varied over the years. During depressions these people argue in favour of government cuts, to enable the private sector to save more, and therefore to spend more. In the 1930's we saved ourselves right into ten years of misery. Government reductions in expenditures are supposed to stimulate the economy, but these people argue today that government cuts are a means of restraining the economy.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
It looks as though the ordinary people of this country never win. The impression is clearly that those who hold money want the government to abdicate the management of the nation to them, and leave the setting of priorities only to those who hold the money. George Bain put it very well in a recent article in the Globe and Mail when he said this about the Minister of Finance:
And, yet, when the finance minister speaks of its being necessary to restrain our collective demands on the capital market, the emphasis clearly is on the public sector. There is no corresponding pressure to restrain the demands of the builders of shopping centres, office buildings, hotels and motels, and the like. Private spending is good spending; public spending is, if not bad spending, at least suspect spending.
Most budgets that come before this house are pretty murky documents. The one introduced by the Minister of Finance last week is painfully clear, however, because it indicates that the government is clearly in a state
5188	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Saltsman of crisis. If only the Liberal party were in this position perhaps we would not be terribly concerned, because there seem to be others on that side of the house and on this who are only too anxious to take over. The members of the official opposition have had a hand in bringing us to the brink of national suicide. This may be harsh criticism, even in a house where punches are not pulled, but we have only to read the budget to get a feeling of despair for the future.
Of all the problems facing the Minister of Finance, the most urgent is obviously money. He needs money, and he needs it badly. It is not difficult to see why. If we look at the refunding program for next year we find it is about twice as great as it has been in recent years. We have a strange situation. In 1950 the Liberals issued bonds due in 1968 in the amount of $308 million. The Conservatives when in office were aware that this amount of money would have to be paid out in 1968, but added $1.2 billion.
When I hear members of the official opposition call for fiscal responsibility, I wonder how responsible that kind of action was. It meant that at that time $1.3 billion would have to be refunded in one year. Then the Liberals came back into office. In 1964 and 1966 they added another $696 million to be refunded in the year 1968. So we have a situation lacing the Minister of Finance next year in which he must find over $2 billion in the marketplace to refund the issues that will then become due.
I have no way of knowing for certain how much money the Minister of Finance has to find in the way of three month, six month and ten month treasury bills, but the indication is that it might be an equivalent amount. We must recognize that the government has its problems. It has problems in terms of controlling its own expenditures. We see what happens when it starts making massive cuts; the good goes out with the bad, because it seems that when the government tries to satisfy everyone they have to satisfy them that all the sacred cows or all the priorities will not be touched.
The government has limited control over the actions of the provinces. It refuses to set up, or cannot for one reason or another set up private spending priorities. It does not seem able or willing to do anything about productivity in this country. Much more than that, the greatest liability of the government is its own dogma that does not permit it to move from the nineteenth century into the

DEBATES	December 7, 1967
twentieth century. Can we manage this nation with outworn ideas? Can we continue to count on over-all fiscal and monetary policy alone to cure the difficulties facing us today? I do not think we can. I suggest that the government will have to move into new types of programs, into more selective programs in order to cure these problems. If we look at the euphemisms in the speech of the Minister of Finance we get a clear indication of why his ideas will not solve the difficulties facing us today. Let me quote from the minister's speech, where he said:
We expect to see a better performance In overall productivity, partly as a consequence of better training and deployment of our labour force and partly because there Is usually an increase in productivity at this stage of the business cycle.
If you translate that into ordinary words, it means that the minister is going to create unemployment in order to try and hold prices down. When the minister says there has been a rapid economic expansion in recent years, he is not giving the full information that is necessary, because Canada has fared very badly compared with other nations in the world. When he says, "This would require the exercise of restraint on increases in prices, wages, other money incomes such as rent and dividends, and government expenditures", he seems to have control, and is willing to exercise that control, only over government expenditures.
How does he propose to exercise restraint on prices? The minister has no mechanism for restraint on prices. I suggest to him that he needs such mechanism. We have been urging the government to establish a prices review board for this purpose. How does the minister intend to exercise restraint over rents and dividends? What mechanism does he have to do this? He has tried to force interest rates down. Up until now he has not been very successful, and most people who have been predicting the future in this respect do not think he will be successful in the future.
The minister may pray. He figures that if nothing else works, he can pray. Prayer is a very powerful weapon, but I do not think it is powerful enough to cure the problems which face the minister. He will have to do more than just pray. It seems to me that in this respect there is the saying that help comes to those who help themselves.

The Budget-Mr. Mackasey that we have one of the highest levels of savings in the world. Socialism may have its application in developing countries, and in communist countries, but it has no place in the Canadian economy. It is significant that when the hon. member for Waterloo South and the hon. member for York South spouted socialist propaganda tonight they did not refer to a freeze in salaries. They know it is impossible and they know it is not palatable to labour. They know that it is against the spirit of the British North America Act, and yet time after time they get up in this House of Commons with sanctimonious arguments that are against the interests of the people of this country. Canadians know, Mr. Speaker, that the economy of Canada has never been in greater shape.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
I wish I had more time because I really want to talk about my Tory friends, who dissipated the greatest majority in Canadian history in 1958 and bankrupted the unemployment insurance fund in 1962.
